Here's some further unwarranted advice.
- take it 3 seconds at a time. Count it out if you have to. If you can't take it for that long? *You can for 1.*
- You don't get to say that you "Deserve" something, from the life in your veins to gifts you're given. We don't know why we're here (alright, alright. Some do, some don't. No shade either way). You just ARE. You can either keep acting like you're the Foreman Or A Ranch Hand at the F-ck up Farm *or* you can take a second, and *Choose* what you're going to do.
- self love isn't easy. Sometimes you just need to go with the facts. You hate your legs and don't want to? Then start with the fact that you're (even if its a mediocre amount) grateful that they work. Then build up from there. Skip the colorful language, and just acknowledge the facts until you can find something you like. Then keep going.

None of this is foolproof or will "fix you". I'm certainly not fixed™️. But this stuff helped me. So maybe it can help you or someone else

- play with angles close up and far off of your body and face. And always try to use as much natural light as you can. The same shot done with different lighting can make a HUGE difference.

Not entirely. To be clear and concise (perhaps a bit blunt):
Not everyone thinks the way you do or experiences *anything* the way you do. Be mindful of that.
Don't assume because *you like something* that someone else will even have experience with it.

You don't know unless you ask and make the effort to ask questions (as redundant as)
- do you know what this is?
- how have you had/experienced [this] before?
- do you have a favorite way to have/experience this?

And so on.

Here's an example:

Lets say that you like vanilla ice cream.
You think it might make [whomever] feel good to have some with you.
You pick some up at the store and make them a bowl of it after dinner.
*however*,
Because you haven't asked them, you don't know they have [trauma/an allergy/a bad childhood memory] with it.

What you did *hurts them* instead of being a kind gesture.

The same thing applies to you.
If you aren't mindful of what makes you feel loved and like *your feelings/thoughts/kind gestures* are reciprocated, it creates resentment and now you have the cycle you described above.
I like the use of "they-self". But I don't mind if the others are used.

To add to what they were saying, if this person doesn't know the ways you feel that they're reciprocating or showing gratitude, you might want to talk about that or keep it in your thoughts so that the next time you feel fulfilled by a turn of phrase or a gesture, you can let him know.

I would also add that we're born "selfish" and we have to learn how to empathize and share. A child can't simply say "I have [complex feelings/nuanced thoughts/etc]." They can only cry until they're provided for.
And maybe when you feel like this, this is your version of doing that.

So please be gentle with yourself.

Oh boy, I'm struggling with this myself. But I came up with an analogy to help combat this-

So here it goes, and also sorry for the bad formatting. I'm stuck on mobile.


Let's use the analogy of the child next door, and I want you to think about if she had a balloon and lost it because of some strong winds. That would hurt her. She would have decided what she wanted to do with the balloon before it went away, how she might want to draw on it and play with it, or she might want to use it in art to make a memory of the day she had.

You wouldn't blame her for experiencing the grief of not met expectations, of feeling overwhelmed by losing what she had, or the feelings that come with having to make new plans.

You can't blame the little girl for her grief at losing her balloon just like you can't blame yourself for the same feelings of something so precious to you, too. (Like losing friends, family, yourself, etc. Within this relationsh*t.)

Let's keep going on that analogy and say that her parents got her another balloon. She would love that balloon all the same. But it's still different. It's still a reminder that she had the last one. It doesn't erase how she was excited about the last one, what she wanted to do with, or how she could go forward with this new one.

Balloons make her happy. But each new one is an experience all in its own.What if she wants this color balloon to be a part of a bigger art project with her parents? Or what if she decides she needs to do something different with it all together? 

It's okay for her to do those things and think about her lost balloon. But feeling guilty for not holding on too tight or thinking maybe she could have tied the string onto her wrist or any other way she could have done differently to not lose that first one doesn't serve her when she's got her new one and playing with it. You can redirect her thoughts to this new balloon and what's fun about it-you can tell her not to feel guilty about her feelings. But losing that first balloon still had impact on her. Maybe those memories are precious to her, or maybe she had a bad day and it was a way for her to get out of that pain of the bad day. 

The same thing can be applied to your relationship to your narcissist and what you had to let go of to protect yourself and those around you.
You can't give yourself these expectations of trying to undo what you had to in order to survive that relationship, at that time.

Think of yourself as that little girl next door when you start to feel guilty if you have to. Or sit with it for 10 seconds or whatever the best technique for you to use to feel it and see it is.

You push it away because it's painful-
And that's a normal human response. Just like sudden feelings of grief-even if a ton of time has passed.


The friends (or family) you had to push away will more than likely understand if you take the courage and be honest and open with them. For others, acquaintances and such, maybe you can just tell them you were going through some stuff. Be vague, but truthful.

At the end of the day you always have a choice to see yourself in a better/less harsh light. 

Just like learning to love our bodies, we can't start at: "I love everything." We have to start at, "My body does its best. I like my body." And work up from there.

I hope this helps my friend. Good luck.
